tier_reason: The memx docs tables (docs/README.memmem.md and siblings) compare memx against libc_* rows for glibc and musl, the harness is public (memx xbench/benches/bench-memmem.rs, bench-memcpy.rs, create_data.rs, driven by makefile.build), the compiler is stated (rustc 1.69.0), the bench profile flags are in memx Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto) and the CPU is named (i5-4570), so tier A stands; the downgrade is for the overstated claim, not the tier.

corrections.workload: Criterion time per pass (200 samples, 100 ms warm-up, 1 s measurement; cache lines flushed before each function's run) over a fixed set of text lines, each pass making many calls, not time per single call: memmem searches the 48-byte needle 'just before we went into the very simple problem' in 21 alternating English lines (en, 10 matches) or a 39-byte Japanese needle in 21 Japanese lines (ja); memchr scans for 'r' (768 matches on en); memcpy copies a 15-byte (en) or 144-byte (ja) source into successive slices of the lines. Built for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-unknown-linux-musl from memx xbench/benches/*.rs; the libc_* rows call the C library through Rust FFI.
corrections.claimed_speedup: memx-cdy README: 'Faster os libc and musl libc'. Derived from page data (memx docs tables, Intel i5-4570, rustc 1.69.0, Criterion time per pass, libc divided by memx): memmem gnu:en 2.173 vs 0.798 us (2.7x), gnu:ja 3.828 vs 1.230 us (3.1x), musl:en 3.948 vs 0.794 us (5.0x), musl:ja 7.010 vs 1.197 us (5.9x); memchr gnu 1.09x and 1.07x (4.849 vs 4.451, 5.764 vs 5.402 us), musl 2.0x and 1.9x (8.757 vs 4.426, 10.205 vs 5.322 us); memcmp musl:en 1.14x and musl:ja 3.8x (8.653 vs 2.293 us) but slower on glibc (gnu:en 1.584 vs 2.828 us, 0.56x; gnu:ja 1.582 vs 2.022 us, 0.78x); memset gnu:ja 1.14x and musl:ja 1.50x but slower on the short en case (gnu:en 2.003 vs 3.388 us, 0.59x; musl:en 2.139 vs 3.515 us, 0.61x). memcpy: memx is 3.1x faster than musl on en (20.289 vs 6.527 us) and 1.55x on ja, but 0.50x of glibc on en (3.483 vs 7.016 us) and 0.96x on ja; memx-cdy does not deliver the musl memcpy win, because its memcpy export is compiled out on musl targets and by the default 'no_memcpy' feature.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmarks on a 2013-era desktop CPU with rustc 1.69 (2023); memx is now 0.2.2 (2026) and the tables were not regenerated with a date, so they may not reflect current code. glibc and musl versions are not stated. The benchmark times the memx Rust functions directly, not memx-cdy's C ABI exports or the LD_PRELOAD path; the wrappers add slice construction and memcmp switches to a byte loop for n < 4. memx-cdy's memcpy is exported only on non-musl targets and only when the default 'no_memcpy' feature is disabled (src/lib.rs notes a duplicate-symbol link error on musl), so the memcpy musl rows do not apply to it, and on glibc memx's memcpy is slower on short copies. Timings are per pass over 21 text lines with many short calls each, so per-call overhead (FFI and PLT for libc_*) weighs heavily; musl's memchr, memmem and memcpy are simple C, so the musl gaps largely reflect musl's weakness. memx's own harness calls memchr::memmem::find per call (building a searcher each time), which is why the memchr crate's memmem row is about 4x slower than glibc; treat the memmem comparison with care. One Criterion table per function, no confidence intervals reported. Benchmark code and docs live in the memx repository, not memx-cdy.

notes: Tier A kept; downgraded for overstatement: the memcpy musl 3.1x figure cannot be obtained through memx-cdy (memcpy export compiled out on musl and by the default no_memcpy feature), timings are per pass not per call, and memset/memcmp are slower than glibc on the short case. Real wins are memmem (2.7-5.9x over glibc and musl) and memchr/memcmp over musl; versus glibc only memmem is clearly faster. memx itself was already folded into this entry as a duplicate.

tier_reason: The X60 results pages carry 'libc' and 'musl' rows next to the RVV variants, the harness and kernels are public (bench/memcpy.c, memcpy.S, memset.c, memset.S, strlen.c, strlen.S, bench.h, config.h), flags are in config.mk (-march=rv64gcv -O3 -DUSE_PERF_EVENT), the CPU is named (SpacemiT X60, 1.6 GHz, VLEN 256) and the run is pinned to rvv-bench commit e1b462f; the compiler is only given by the 'scalar_autovec_clang18' label, which suffices for hand-written assembly, so tier A stands. Downgrade is for the overstated strlen claim.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No headline number in the README; the numbers are in the per-board results pages. Derived from page data (SpacemiT X60 results, fixed variant rvv_m4 against the libc row, bytes/cycle at the nearest recorded size): memcpy 4.73x at 66 B (1.941 vs 0.410), 2.71x at about 1 KB (4.298 vs 1.585), 2.71x at about 16 KB (5.040 vs 1.860), 2.05x at about 265 KB (3.438 vs 1.674), 1.07-1.11x at 8-64 MB; never below libc over all 233 sizes (geomean 2.0x). memset 3.55x at 66 B, 1.64x at about 1 KB, 1.72x at about 16 KB, 1.79x at about 265 KB, parity (1.00-1.02x) from 8 MB up (geomean 1.5x over 245 sizes). strlen is noisy and mixed: 1.36x at 61 B (but 0.72x at 55 B and 1.15x at 67 B), 1.81x at about 1 KB, 2.44x at about 16 KB; the 2.89x at about 260 KB is an isolated spike (0.65x at 245 KB, 0.95x at 275 KB), and above about 280 KB rvv_m4 is slower than libc (about 0.30 vs 0.45 B/cycle, 0.65-0.7x); rvv_m4 is slower than libc at 135 of 262 strlen sizes (geomean 1.15x). Other strlen variants do better: rvv_m1 stays about 2x libc at multi-MB sizes (0.98 vs 0.46 B/cycle at 3.6 MB) and rvv_page_aligned_m8 reaches 4.9x at 16 KB (6.388 vs 1.308 B/cycle), a best-variant selection.
corrections.hardware: SpacemiT X60 cores of the SpacemiT K1 (Banana Pi BPI-F3), 1.6 GHz, RVV 1.0 with VLEN 256, for the figures quoted; the results repository also has folders for SiFive P870, XuanTie C920V2, SpacemiT A100 and X100, Tenstorrent X280 and others, Sipeed Lichee Pi 4A, CanMV K230 and more
corrections.caveats: The baseline is whatever libc the board ran (distribution and version not recorded; most likely a scalar glibc without an RVV string path), so much of the gap is the absence of RVV code in that libc, not a better algorithm; the author's own observations on the X60 index page compare against musl's SWAR code. Ratios are derived from the chart data embedded in the results HTML at the nearest recorded size, for one fixed variant; best-variant figures are selections. Each point is the median of 10 to 64 repeats (bench/config.h MIN_REPEATS 10, MAX_REPEATS 64) with output validated against a reference on the first repetition, but no spread is shown, and strlen in the 30-400 KB range swings between 0.33x and 3.5x of libc from one size to the next. memcpy and memset gains shrink to parity once data leaves the caches (8 MB and up). The compiler is only identified by the 'scalar_autovec_clang18' label; config.mk's default is CC=cc. The rendered results site is on github.io (blocked here), so the HTML in the rvv-bench-results repository was parsed. Other kernels in the repo (utf8_count, memreverse, mergelines, byteswap, base64) have no libc counterpart and are not part of this claim. The routines are benchmark kernels in bench/*.S, not a packaged library.

notes: Tier A kept; downgraded because the strlen figures were cherry-picked: 2.89x at 260 KB is a single noisy point and rvv_m4 strlen is slower than libc at more than half the recorded sizes and at every size above about 280 KB. memcpy (geomean 2.0x, never slower) and memset (1.5x in cache, parity in DRAM) hold up. Baseline libc identity and version are unrecorded.

tier_reason: results/README.md and the raw .dat files under results/raw/G3E compare the proposed SVE routines with GNU libc and Arm optimized-routines 23.01; the harness and routines are public (src/bench.c, src/driver.c, src/main.c, string/aarch64/new/*.S, CMakeLists.txt with -march=armv8.4-a+sve), the compiler (GCC 12.3.0) and CPU (AWS Graviton3E, hpc7g.16xlarge) are stated. I re-derived every quoted geomean from the .dat median runtimes and they match.

corrections.workload: Median per-call runtime (101 samples, each the average of an inner repeat loop, after warm-up calls, hot cache, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW) and bandwidth of string routines on random alphanumeric buffers: short strings 1 to 128 B in steps of 1, and a full range of 24 sizes doubling from 64 B to 512 MiB (the README says 128 B, the .dat files start at 64 B), aligned and unaligned allocations, on an AWS Graviton3E.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: the proposed SVE implementations 'never' regress against Arm optimized-routines and 'are competitive with their GNU libc counterparts, namely: strcpy, strncpy, strcmp and strncmp'. Derived from page data (raw .dat median runtimes, glibc time divided by proposed time, geometric mean over buffer sizes, aligned/unaligned): 64 B to 512 MiB strcpy 1.64x/1.61x, strncpy 1.40x/1.39x, strcmp 1.37x/1.32x, strncmp 1.45x/1.43x; 1 to 128 B strncpy 1.63x/1.58x, strcpy 1.32x/1.13x (unaligned dips to 0.37x at some lengths), strncmp 1.19x/1.18x, strcmp 1.13x/1.13x (as low as 0.55x at some short lengths). Against Arm optimized-routines 23.01 at 64 B to 512 MiB (derived): strcpy 2.8x, strlen 3.0x, strcmp 1.8x. The README lists memcpy, memcmp, strlen, strnlen, strchr and strrchr as inconclusive (memcpy geomean 0.76x of glibc at full sizes, strlen 0.94x). On NVIDIA Grace (results/raw/Grace, labelled glibc 2.34, derived, aligned full range) the gains shrink: strcpy 1.06x, strcmp 1.01x, strncmp 1.35x, strncpy 1.35x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.3.0 on kernel 6.2.0-1018-aws; CMake C11 build with target_compile_options -march=armv8.4-a+sve and no optimization level (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release is commented out, so the C harness builds at GCC's default -O0); the measured routines are hand-written .S files, so the driver flags matter little; -DSHORT_STRS, -DFULL_SIZE_RANGE, -DALIGNED_ALLOCS and -DCMP_LIBC select the modes
corrections.license: LGPL-3.0 (repository LICENSE and harness sources); the routine sources derived from Arm optimized-routines keep Arm's header 'SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception' (checked in string/aarch64/new/strcpy-sve.S)
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is by the authors of the new routines (research group, not independent). Hot-cache repeated calls with warm-up, so cold-cache and branch-predictor effects are not covered. The win comes from replacing SVE INCx with CNTx plus ADD, a Neoverse V1 latency issue: on NVIDIA Grace (Neoverse V2) the same harness shows strcpy 1.06x and strcmp 1.01x over glibc. glibc runs its own NEON/generic implementations on Graviton3E (the README mentions the NEON strcmp), not SVE ones. The 'GNU libc 2.39' name is a hard-coded label in src/main.c; the kernel 6.2.0-1018-aws suggests an Ubuntu release whose stock glibc is older, so the measured glibc version is not confirmed. Correctness asserts in src/main.c run only under -DDEBUG, which the CMakeLists never adds (its 'EQUAL Debug' test is a numeric comparison), so the timed builds do not check results. Short unaligned strcpy has lengths where the new routine is up to 2.7x slower than glibc (the README acknowledges drops). The ratios are derived by the reporter from results/raw/G3E/*/*.dat; the README itself only gives qualitative statements, plots and a truncated sample table. One size in the unaligned full-range strncpy data lacks a usable pair (23 of 24 sizes usable).

notes: Confirmed at A; every quoted geomean reproduces from the .dat files. Added the Grace cross-check (gains largely vanish on Neoverse V2 for strcpy/strcmp), the unverified glibc 2.39 label, the -O0 harness and DEBUG-only correctness checks, and the per-file Arm licence on the routines.
